title: How to Bake Sourdough English Muffins in Large Batches
meta_description: Learn how to batch bake sourdough English muffins fast and effortlessly. Get step‑by‑step tips, dough handling tricks, and why Silicone Baking Mats are a game‑c
html:
If you’re looking to batch bake sourdough English muffins for a brunch crowd or meal‑prep stash, you’re in the right place. This guide walks you through scaling a classic recipe, mastering the dough, and using tools like Silicone Baking Mats to keep things tidy and consistent.

Why Batch Baking Sourdough English Muffins Works

Making a single dozen can feel like a chore, but scaling up to 3‑4 dozen saves time and reduces waste. The sourdough starter adds flavor and keeps the muffins airy, while the larger batch lets you use the same dough to fill a whole week’s worth of breakfasts. When you batch bake sourdough English muffins, you also get a more uniform rise because the dough rests longer between shaping and cooking.

Scaling the Recipe: Ingredients for 48 Muffins

Start with a healthy starter (100% hydration) and multiply the base recipe by four. Here’s a solid foundation:

  1. 8 cups (960 g) bread flour
  2. 1 ½ cups (360 g) active sourdough starter
  3. 2 ½ cups (600 ml) warm milk
  4. ¼ cup (56 g) granulated sugar
  5. ¼ cup (56 g) melted butter
  6. 2 tbsp (30 g) salt
  7. 2 tbsp (30 g) baking soda (added just before cooking)
  8. Oil for greasing the griddle

Mix the flour, starter, milk, sugar, butter, and salt until a shaggy dough forms. Let it rest 30 minutes (autolyse), then knead briefly until smooth. Cover and ferment at room temperature for 4‑6 hours, or refrigerate overnight for a deeper flavor.

Shaping and Preparing the Muffins

When the dough has doubled, turn it out onto a lightly floured surface. Pat it to about ½‑inch thickness and use a 3‑inch round cutter to cut circles. Don’t over‑handle the dough; a gentle press keeps the interior light. Place the rounds on a tray lined with Silicone Baking Mats. The mats provide a non‑stick surface, eliminate the need for parchment, and make cleanup a breeze—especially useful when you’re handling dozens of muffins.

Cooking the Muffins on a Griddle

Heat a heavy‑bottomed griddle or large skillet over medium‑low heat. Lightly oil the surface—just a thin brush will do. Transfer the muffins (still on the silicone mats) to the griddle, leaving space between each piece. Cook for 3‑4 minutes per side, until golden brown and the tops are set. Sprinkle a little baking soda on the cooking surface for the last batch; it helps create those classic nooks and crannies.

Storing and Reheating for Maximum Freshness

Once cooled, split the muffins with a fork (not a knife) to preserve the texture. Store them in an airtight container or zip‑top bag in the fridge for up to 5 days. To reheat, toast lightly or microwave for 10‑15 seconds. If you’ve baked a surplus, freeze the split muffins on a silicone baking mat, then transfer to a freezer bag. They toast up perfectly straight from frozen.

FAQ

Can I use a stand‑mixier for the dough?

Yes. Use the dough hook on low speed until the ingredients combine, then increase to medium for 2‑3 minutes to develop gluten. Avoid over‑mixing, which can make the muffins tough.

Do I need to dust the silicone baking mats with flour?

No. The non‑stick surface keeps the dough from sticking, but a light dusting of flour can help you see the edges of each muffin when you’re shaping a large batch.

What’s the best way to achieve the signature “nooks and crannies”?

After cooking, press the tops of the muffins with a fork while they’re still warm. This opens up the interior and creates the classic texture that makes English muffins so versatile.
